jer49.d: Gentile believers need not be circumcised or keep the whole Law (Acts 15; compare Galatians 2).

arles314.d: Rejected the Donatist appeal; ruled that baptism by heretics in the name of the Trinity is not repeated.

nic1.d: Condemned Arius; creed with homoousios (“of one substance”); common date of Easter; 20 canons.

serdica.d: Western bishops upheld Athanasius; canons allowing appeals to the bishop of Rome.

con1.d: Confirmed Nicaea, confessed the divinity of the Holy Spirit; the creed now called Nicene; canon 3 ranked Constantinople after Rome.

carth397.d: Listed the books of Scripture, including the deuterocanonical books (repeating Hippo, 393).

eph431.d: Deposed Nestorius; upheld Mary as Theotokos, “God-bearer”.

eph449.d: Restored Eutyches and deposed Flavian; annulled by Chalcedon.

chalc.d: Christ one person “in two natures”; Leo’s Tome received; canon 28 on Constantinople (rejected by Rome).

con2.d: Condemned the “Three Chapters”; read Chalcedon in the light of Cyril.

tol589.d: The Visigoths renounced Arianism; the creed was recited with the Filioque.

con3.d: Christ has two wills and two operations; condemned Monothelitism, including Pope Honorius.

trullo.d: 102 disciplinary canons; repeated canon 28; criticised some Roman customs.

nic2.d: Restored the veneration of icons, distinguishing it from worship due to God alone.

frank794.d: Rejected Nicaea II as understood from a faulty Latin translation; condemned Adoptionism.

con4.b: few at first, about 100 by the end
con4.d: Condemned Photius; counted by the West as the Eighth Ecumenical Council.

con879.d: Restored Photius and reconciled him with Rome; forbade adding to the creed. Many Orthodox regard it as the eighth council.

lat4.d: Defined transubstantiation; required yearly confession and communion; regulated Jews and heretics.

lyon2.d: Short-lived union with the Byzantine emperor; defined the Filioque “as from one principle”.

constance.d: Ended the Western Schism (Martin V, 1417); condemned Hus; declared council authority (Haec sancta).

florence.d: Union with the Greeks (1439), later Armenians and Copts; rejected by most Orthodox at home.

trent.by: Paul III, Julius III, Pius IV
trent.d: Scripture and tradition; justification; seven sacraments; Mass as sacrifice; reform of bishops and seminaries.

dort.d: The Canons of Dort against the Remonstrants: the “five points” of Calvinism.

jassy.d: Approved Peter Mogila’s Orthodox Confession, answering Calvinist and Catholic influences.

westm.d: Westminster Confession and Catechisms, the standards of Presbyterian churches.

jer1672.d: Confession of Dositheos rejecting the Calvinist confession attributed to Cyril Lucaris.

vat1.d: Faith and reason; papal primacy and infallibility (Pastor aeternus).

mos1917.d: Restored the patriarchate (Tikhon) on the eve of Soviet persecution.

vat2.d: Liturgy in the vernacular; the Church; revelation; ecumenism; religious liberty; relations with Jews and other religions.

crete.d: Documents on mission, marriage, fasting and ecumenism; Moscow, Antioch, Bulgaria and Georgia stayed away.

east: Patriarchal see now in Erbil; the historic Church of the East.

oriental: Patriarchate of Alexandria; the largest Christian body in the Middle East.
Patriarchate of Antioch, seated in Damascus since 1959.
Indian Saint Thomas Christians; catholicate established 1912.
orthodox: Patriarchates of Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem
Autocephalous 1448; patriarchate from 1589; the largest Orthodox church.
Autocephalous since the Council of Ephesus (431).
Churches of Poland, Albania, and the Czech Lands and Slovakia
Orthodox Church in America and Orthodox Church of Ukraine
Autocephaly granted 1970 (by Moscow) and 2019 (by Constantinople); recognition is disputed.
ecath: From the Union of Brest (1595–96); the largest Eastern Catholic church.
Saint Thomas Christians in communion with Rome.
Lebanon’s Syriac church, never in separate communion according to its own tradition.
Byzantine-rite Antiochenes united with Rome in 1724.
Chaldean, Syro-Malankara, Armenian, Coptic, Syriac and Ethiopian Catholic churches
Among the 23 Eastern churches sui iuris in communion with Rome.
catholic: The Western church of the Roman rite, with variants such as the Ambrosian rite of Milan.
Self-governing churches with their own rites, also in communion with Rome.
Benedictines, Franciscans, Dominicans, Jesuits and many others.
oldcath: Old Catholic churches in the Netherlands, Germany, Switzerland, Austria, the Czech Republic and Poland.
Founded in the United States in 1897; left the Union of Utrecht in 2003.
lutheran: Church of Sweden, Church of Norway and other Nordic churches
Ethiopian Mekane Yesus and Tanzanian Lutheran churches
reformed: Church of Scotland, Presbyterian Church (USA), Presbyterian churches of Korea.
Such as the Protestant Church in the Netherlands (2004) and the Reformed Church in Hungary.
Unions such as the United Church of Canada (1925) and the Church of South India (1947), with Methodists and Anglicans.
anabaptist: Followers of Menno Simons; the Mennonite World Conference.
Church of the Brethren and the Bruderhof
Later movements in the Anabaptist tradition.
anglican: About 42 provinces in communion with the Archbishop of Canterbury.
Churches of Nigeria, Uganda and Kenya
Among the largest Anglican provinces today.
GAFCON and the Anglican Church in North America
baptist: Baptist conventions of Nigeria and elsewhere
Growing churches in Africa, Asia and Latin America.
methodist: Fellowship of Methodist and Wesleyan churches.
Formed 2022 by congregations leaving the United Methodist Church.
Such as the Church of the Nazarene and The Salvation Army.
pente: One of the oldest Pentecostal denominations.
Such as the Redeemed Christian Church of God (1952) and the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God (1977).
Pentecostal-style spirituality within other churches, including Catholic Charismatic Renewal (1967).
